Make Love, Not War
MAYK LUV, not WOR
slogan (Boomer slang)
The anti-Vietnam War slogan of the mid-1960s, printed on buttons, posters, and placards by 1965–67. The folklorist Gershon Legman claimed to have coined it in a 1963 lecture at Ohio University; whatever its first speaker, its power lay in pairing the sexual revolution with the peace movement in four words. It was everywhere at the 1967 Summer of Love and remained the defining slogan of the era.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Make love, not war was the counterculture’s whole creed on a button: the war in Vietnam was the work of repressed, uptight old men, and the cure was free sexual love among the young. The Christian observation: the slogan uses the holiest word in the language to mean its cheapest counterfeit, and it gets the source of war exactly backwards. James asks the question the slogan thought it had answered: "From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" (Jas 4:1). War does not come from too little appetite; it comes from appetite unruled. The free love of the 1960s did not end the fighting; it moved the battlefield into the home, and the children of broken marriages inherited the casualties. Scripture’s love is another thing entirely. "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up" (1Co 13:4). Its highest act is not a night but a death: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends" (Joh 15:13). And God’s will for the body is plain: "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication" (1Th 4:3). The Christian does not answer the slogan with "make war"; he answers with the love that keeps covenant — the only love that has ever brought peace into a house.

Webster 1828 Definition

The mid-1960s anti-war slogan pairing the peace movement with the sexual revolution — a creed Scripture overturns, since wars come from lusts (Jas 4:1) and true love lays down its life (Joh 15:13).

MAKE LOVE, NOT WAR, slogan (Boomer era, c. 1965–67) The anti-Vietnam War motto of the counterculture, urging sexual freedom and pacifism in place of militarism. Printed on buttons and placards; chanted at demonstrations.

Webster (1828) — LOVE, noun 1. An affection of the mind excited by beauty and worth of any kind, or by the qualities of an object which communicate pleasure, sensual or intellectual. It is opposed to hatred. love between the sexes, is a compound affection, consisting of esteem, benevolence, and animal desire. love is excited by pleasing qualities of any kind, as by kindness, benevolence, charity, and by the qualities which render social intercourse agreeable. In the latter case, love is ardent friendship, or a strong attachment springing from good will and esteem, and the pleasure derived from the company, civilities and kindness of others. Between certain natural relatives, love seems to be in some cases instinctive. Such is the love of a mother for her child, which manifests itself toward an infant, before any particular qualities in the child are unfolded.

Webster (1828) — WAR, noun [G., to perplex, embroil, disturb. The primary sense of the root is to strive, struggle, urge, drive, or to turn, to twist.] 1. A contest between nations or states, carried on by force, either for defense, or for revenging insults and redressing wrongs, for the extension of commerce or acquisition of territory, or for obtaining and establishing the superiority and dominion of one over the other. These objects are accomplished by the slaughter or capture of troops, and the capture and destruction of ships, towns and property. Among rude nations, war is often waged and carried on for plunder. As war is the contest of nations or states, it always implies that such contest is authorized by the monarch or the sovereign power of the nation. When war is commenced by attacking a nation in peace, it si called an offensive war and such attack is aggressive.

Decode for families: make love here does not mean what your great-grandmother meant by it (to court, to woo). The slogan is the sexual revolution in four words.

Key Scripture

Jas 4:1 — "From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?"

1Co 13:4 — "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,"

Joh 15:13 — "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends."

1Th 4:3 — "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication:"

Gal 5:13 — "For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another."

Modern Corruption

The slogan names lust as love and repression as the cause of war; Scripture names lust as the cause of war (Jas 4:1) and covenant self-giving as love.

expand to see more

Notice what happens to the word love. In 1828 to make love meant to court a woman with a view to marriage. By 1967 it meant sexual intercourse with anyone, anywhere, without covenant. The slogan finished the theft: it took the word for the highest thing and pinned it to the appetite, then offered the appetite as the remedy for violence. But appetite is the root of violence. "Come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" (Jas 4:1). The generation that was told to make love instead of war got both — the war in Southeast Asia and a second war fought in family courts for the next fifty years.

Paul has the true pairing. "Ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another" (Gal 5:13). Liberty for the flesh is the slogan; liberty for service is the gospel. A father tells his son: the strongest man in the room is not the one who takes what he wants but the one who lays down his life for his friends (Joh 15:13) — and for his wife, and for his children. That love ends wars.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English lufu (love) + Old English werre / Old French werre (war); make love = to court (17th–19th c.) → to have sex (20th c.) → mid-1960s anti-war slogan.

expand to see more

Old English lufu — love, affection; Greek agapē (Joh 15:13) — self-giving love

Late Old English werre, from Old North French werre (Frankish werra, confusion, strife)

17th–19th c.: to make love — to pay court, to woo

20th c.: to make love — to have sexual intercourse

c. 1965–67: Make love, not war on anti-Vietnam buttons and placards

Usage

""Grandpa still has the button: MAKE LOVE NOT WAR. Grandma made him put it in a drawer.""

"Wars come from lusts that war in our members (Jas 4:1); the slogan prescribed the disease as the cure."

"Greater love hath no man than this (Joh 15:13) — love that dies for its friends, not love that uses them."
